topics.10: What the cell membrane is made of
topics.20: All the words for head / tail

questions.q: Which plane divides the body into front (anterior) and back (posterior) portions?
questions.e: The coronal (frontal) plane splits front from back.

questions.q: Which plane is also called the horizontal plane?
questions.e: Transverse = horizontal plane; it divides top from bottom.

questions.q: Which plane divides the body into EQUAL left and right halves?
questions.e: The midsagittal (median) plane runs directly through the center.

questions.q: The transverse plane divides the body into:
questions.e: Transverse (horizontal) = superior vs. inferior.

questions.q: The coronal plane is also known as the:
questions.e: Coronal a.k.a. frontal.

questions.q: A plane that divides the body into UNEQUAL left and right pieces is a:
questions.e: Sagittal = left/right pieces; midsagittal is the special case that makes equal halves.

questions.q: The midsagittal plane is a special type of which plane?
questions.e: Midsagittal (median) = a sagittal plane through the exact center.

questions.q: Which plane divides the body at various angles?
questions.e: Oblique (angular) plane cuts at various angles.

questions.q: Anatomy is the study of the body's:
questions.e: Anatomy = STRUCTURE (names of parts and regions).

questions.q: Physiology is the study of:
questions.e: Physiology = how the body FUNCTIONS and how parts work together.

questions.q: Describing HOW the kidneys filter waste from blood is an example of:
questions.e: How something works = function = physiology.

questions.q: Learning the names of the bones of the skull is an example of:
questions.e: Names of parts = structure = anatomy.

questions.q: Explaining how the heart pumps blood through the body is:
questions.e: Pumping is a function, so it's physiology.

questions.q: Identifying the four chambers of the heart is:
questions.e: Identifying parts = structure = anatomy.

questions.q: Why are anatomy and physiology studied together?
w: Function determines the names of parts
questions.e: The lecture's spoon/fork/knife example: a part's structure determines what it can do.

questions.q: Which statement is correct?
w: Both mean the study of function
Both mean the study of structure
questions.e: Anatomy = STRUCTURE; physiology = FUNCTION.

questions.q: Losing electrons in a chemical reaction is called:
questions.e: LEO: Lose Electrons = Oxidation.

questions.q: Gaining electrons in a chemical reaction is called:
questions.e: GER: Gain Electrons = Reduction.

questions.q: When sodium (Na) loses an electron and becomes Na⁺, sodium has been:
questions.e: Na loses an electron, so it is oxidized (LEO).

questions.q: When chlorine (Cl) gains an electron and becomes Cl⁻, chlorine has been:
questions.e: Cl gains an electron, so it is reduced (GER).

questions.q: In the memory aid 'LEO the lion goes GER', what does LEO stand for?
questions.e: LEO = Lose Electrons = Oxidation; GER = Gain Electrons = Reduction.

questions.q: Which statement about oxidation and reduction is TRUE?
w: They never occur in the same reaction
questions.e: An oxidation must be coupled with a reduction, and vice versa.

questions.q: In GER, the 'R' stands for:
questions.e: Gain Electrons = Reduction.

questions.q: An atom that becomes more NEGATIVE by picking up an electron has undergone:
questions.e: Gaining an electron (more negative charge) = reduction.

questions.q: Atomic number is equal to the number of:
questions.e: Atomic number = # of protons.

questions.q: Atomic mass is equal to the number of:
questions.e: Atomic mass = protons + neutrons.

questions.q: How do you calculate the number of neutrons in an atom?
questions.e: # neutrons = atomic mass − atomic number.

questions.q: An element has an atomic number of 20. How many electrons are in a neutral atom of it?
questions.e: Neutral atoms have equal protons and electrons, so 20.

questions.q: An atom has 11 protons. How many electrons does a neutral atom of it have?
questions.e: # electrons = # protons in a neutral atom.

questions.q: Which type of bond forms when a metal gives electrons to a nonmetal?
questions.e: Ionic bonds: electrons given by a metal and received by a nonmetal.

questions.q: Which type of bond is described as STRONG?
questions.e: Covalent bonds are STRONG bonds where nonmetals share electrons.

questions.q: Which relatively WEAK bond forms between water molecules and between DNA bases?
questions.e: Hydrogen bonds are relatively weak attractions between H atoms of different molecules.

questions.q: A bond formed between a cation (+) and an anion (−) is a(n):
questions.e: Ionic bonds form between oppositely charged ions.

questions.q: Which type of bond falls apart (dissociates) easily in water?
questions.e: Ionic bonds dissociate easily in water (e.g., NaCl).

questions.q: NaCl (table salt) is held together by which type of bond?
questions.e: NaCl is the lecture's example of an ionic bond.

questions.q: A covalent bond in which electrons are shared EQUALLY (e.g., CO₂) is:
questions.e: Nonpolar covalent = equal sharing; atoms close to the same size.

questions.q: Hydrogen bonds form between:
questions.e: Hydrogen bonds: adjacent hydrogen atoms of DIFFERENT molecules.

questions.q: Which term means 'toward the head'?
questions.e: Superior, cranial and cephalic all mean toward the head.

questions.q: 'Caudal' means:
questions.e: Caudal (caudad) = toward the tail, same as inferior.

questions.q: Which pair of terms BOTH mean 'toward the head'?
questions.e: Head: superior/cranial/cephalic. Tail: inferior/caudal/caudad.

questions.q: 'Superior' is also called:
questions.e: Superior (cranial/cephalic) = toward the head.

questions.q: 'Inferior' is also called:
questions.e: Inferior (caudal/caudad) = toward the tail/feet.

questions.q: The term 'cranial' comes from cranium, which means:
questions.e: Cranium = skull → 'cranial'.

questions.q: Which term means the OPPOSITE of caudal?
questions.e: Caudal = toward tail; cranial = toward head.

questions.q: Which pair of terms BOTH mean 'toward the tail'?
questions.e: Inferior, caudal and caudad all mean toward the tail/feet.

questions.q: The smallest unit of matter is the:
questions.e: Atoms are the smallest unit of matter.

questions.q: The smallest unit of life is the:
questions.e: Cells are the smallest unit of life.

questions.q: Which pairing is correct?
questions.e: Atom = smallest unit of matter; cell = smallest unit of life.

questions.q: The study of cells, the smallest unit of life, is called:
questions.e: Cytology = study of cells. Histology = study of tissues.

questions.q: Atoms are made of which three subatomic particles?
questions.e: Atoms (smallest unit of matter) are made of protons, neutrons and electrons.

questions.q: Which is the correct order from smallest to largest?
questions.e: Levels of organization build from atoms up to the organism.

questions.q: The human body is made of roughly how many cells?
questions.e: The body is made of ~35 trillion cells, the smallest units of life.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT alive on its own, but is the smallest unit of matter?
questions.e: Atoms are matter, not life. The cell is the smallest living unit.

questions.q: Homeostasis is best defined as:
w: The breakdown of food into nutrients
The movement of water across a membrane
questions.e: Homeostasis = the process of maintaining a stable internal environment.

questions.q: Homeostasis is also known as:
questions.e: a.k.a. dynamic equilibrium or state of balance.

questions.q: In a homeostatic feedback loop, which part SENSES the change?
questions.e: Stimulus → receptor (senses) → control center → effector.

questions.q: In a feedback loop, which part interprets the signal and decides how to respond?
questions.e: The control center interprets the signal and sends instructions.

questions.q: In a feedback loop, which part carries out the response (a cell, tissue or organ)?
questions.e: The effector brings about the response; it is always a cell, tissue or organ.

questions.q: In a feedback loop, a 'stimulus' is:
questions.e: Stimulus = deviation from normal.

questions.q: Which organ systems help maintain homeostasis?
questions.e: Virtually every organ system plays a role.

questions.q: What is the correct order of a feedback loop?
questions.e: Stimulus is sensed by a receptor, interpreted by the control center, and carried out by an effector.

questions.q: An acid is a substance that:
questions.e: Acids are H⁺ donors.

questions.q: A base is a substance that:
questions.e: Bases donate OH⁻ and can be defined as H⁺ acceptors.

questions.q: In the reaction HCl → H⁺ + Cl⁻, HCl is acting as:
questions.e: HCl releases H⁺, so it's an acid.

questions.q: In the reaction NaOH → Na⁺ + OH⁻, NaOH is acting as:
questions.e: NaOH releases OH⁻, so it's a base.

questions.q: Which characteristics describe a BASE?
w: Sour taste, burns metal, pH below 7
questions.e: Bases: bitter, slippery, high pH.

questions.q: Which characteristics describe an ACID?
questions.a: Sour taste, burns through metal, pH below 7
questions.e: Acids: sour, burn through metal, low pH.

questions.q: Which substance ACCEPTS hydrogen ions?
questions.e: Bases can be defined as hydrogen ion acceptors.

questions.q: Compounds that resist dramatic changes in pH by adding or removing H⁺ are called:
questions.e: Buffers act as acids when pH is high and as bases when pH is low.

questions.q: What is the MAJOR component of the cell membrane?
questions.e: Phospholipids (bilayer) are the major component.

questions.q: Which TWO types of lipids are found in the cell membrane?
questions.e: Membrane lipids: phospholipids and cholesterol (a steroid).

questions.q: Which is NOT a component of the cell membrane?
questions.e: Membrane = phospholipids, proteins, sugars, cholesterol. Glycogen is stored in liver and muscle.

questions.q: The phospholipid head is ______ and the tail is ______.
questions.e: Head loves water (hydrophilic); tail fears water (hydrophobic).

questions.q: What role does cholesterol play in the cell membrane?
questions.a: Holds phospholipids together; gives flexible rigidity
questions.e: Cholesterol sits between phospholipids and gives 'flexible' rigidity.

questions.q: The 'fluid mosaic model' means membrane components:
questions.a: Are free to move within the membrane
questions.e: Components are not locked in place; they move within the membrane.

questions.q: Which membrane component is used for blood typing?
questions.e: Membrane sugars: cell recognition, receptors, blood typing.

questions.q: Which membrane proteins span the entire membrane and form channels?
questions.e: Integral proteins touch both inside and outside; only they form channels.

questions.q: What is the charge of a neutron?
questions.e: Neutrons have no charge.

questions.q: Which subatomic particle carries a NEGATIVE charge?
questions.e: Electrons are negative.

questions.q: Which subatomic particle carries a POSITIVE charge?
questions.e: Protons are positive.

questions.q: Which correctly matches particle and charge?
questions.e: Proton +, neutron 0, electron −.

questions.q: Which particles are found in the nucleus?
questions.e: Nucleus = protons + neutrons; electrons are in the electron cloud.

questions.q: Where are electrons found?
questions.a: In the electron cloud (shells/orbits) around the nucleus
questions.e: Electrons circle the nucleus in shells, orbits or rings.

questions.q: An atom that LOSES an electron becomes a:
questions.e: Losing electrons leaves more protons, so the atom is positive (cation).

questions.q: An atom that GAINS an electron becomes a(n):
questions.e: Gaining electrons makes it negative (anion).

questions.q: Energy of motion is called:
questions.e: Kinetic = energy of motion.

questions.q: Stored energy is called:
questions.e: Potential = stored energy.

questions.q: Heat, light and the movement of large objects are examples of:
questions.e: All are energy of motion.

questions.q: The energy held in chemical bonds is:
questions.e: Chemical bonds store energy, so it's potential.

questions.q: A charged battery sitting on a shelf contains:
questions.e: A battery is the lecture's example of stored (potential) energy.

questions.q: Energy is defined as:
questions.e: Energy is the ability to do work.

questions.q: A muscle actively contracting and moving the arm shows:
questions.e: Movement = energy of motion = kinetic.

questions.q: Which pairing is correct?
questions.e: Kinetic is motion; potential is stored.

questions.q: H₂ (two hydrogen atoms bonded together) is a:
questions.e: A molecule is one type of element only.

questions.q: A compound is made of:
questions.e: Compound = 2+ different elements.

questions.q: Methane (CH₄), made of carbon and hydrogen, is a:
questions.e: Two different elements make it a compound.

questions.q: O₂ (two oxygen atoms) is best classified as a:
questions.e: Only one type of element (oxygen), so it's a molecule.

questions.q: Water (H₂O) contains hydrogen and oxygen. It is a:
questions.e: Two different elements, so it's a compound.

questions.q: Which is the key difference between a molecule and a compound (as taught in lecture)?
questions.a: Molecule = one type of element; compound = two or more different elements
questions.e: Molecule = same element; compound = multiple elements.

questions.q: Glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆) is a:
questions.e: Three different elements (C, H, O), so it's a compound.

questions.q: N₂ (two nitrogen atoms) is a:
questions.e: One type of element only, so it's a molecule.

questions.q: Which is an example of POSITIVE feedback?
questions.e: Positive feedback examples: childbirth (oxytocin) and blood clotting.

questions.q: In NEGATIVE feedback, the response:
questions.a: Moves in the opposite direction of the change
w: Moves in the same direction as the change
questions.e: Negative feedback counteracts the stimulus.

questions.q: Shivering to warm up when you are cold is an example of:
questions.e: The response opposes the change, so it's negative feedback.

questions.q: Most feedback mechanisms in the body are:
questions.e: Most feedback is negative.

questions.q: In POSITIVE feedback, the response:
questions.e: Positive feedback amplifies and drives farther from normal.

questions.q: Blood clotting is an example of:
questions.e: Blood clotting is a positive feedback example.

questions.q: Sweating when body temperature rises is an example of:
questions.e: Sweating cools the body, opposing the rise.

questions.q: Which hormone drives the positive feedback loop of childbirth?
questions.e: The pituitary releases oxytocin, amplifying contractions.

questions.q: The liquid portion of the cytoplasm is the:
questions.e: Cytoplasm includes cytosol (liquid), organelles, inclusions.

questions.q: Which is NOT part of the cytoplasm?
questions.e: The nucleus is its own component.

questions.q: The three main components of a cell are:
questions.e: Membrane ('skin'), cytoplasm ('guts'), nucleus ('brain').

questions.q: The cytoplasm is described as the cell's:
questions.e: Cytoplasm = the 'guts' of the cell.

questions.q: The nucleus is described as the cell's:
questions.e: Nucleus = 'brain' / command center.

questions.q: Tiny 'organs' inside the cell are called:
questions.e: Organelles = tiny organs within the cytoplasm.

questions.q: Things inside the cytoplasm that do NOT dissolve in water, like fat and pigments, are:
questions.e: Inclusions = undissolved things like fat and pigment.

questions.q: The cytoplasm includes which three things?
questions.e: Cytoplasm = cytosol + organelles + inclusions.

questions.q: Glucose is classified as a:
questions.e: Glucose, fructose, galactose = monosaccharides.

questions.q: Sucrose (glucose + fructose) is a:
questions.e: Disaccharides: sucrose, lactose, maltose.

questions.q: Glycogen, the storage form of glucose in animals, is a:
questions.e: Polysaccharides: starch (plants), glycogen (animals).

questions.q: Lactose is made of:
questions.e: Lactose = glucose + galactose.

questions.q: Maltose is made of:
questions.e: Maltose = glucose + glucose.

questions.q: Starch, the storage form of carbohydrate in plants, is a:
questions.e: Starch = plant polysaccharide.

questions.q: A disaccharide is made of how many monosaccharides?
questions.e: Di = 2.

questions.q: Which chemical reaction joins monosaccharides into a disaccharide?
questions.e: Monosaccharides are combined by dehydration synthesis.

questions.q: Where is glycogen stored in the body?
questions.e: Glycogen is stored in skeletal muscle and liver.

questions.q: Which is a monosaccharide?
questions.e: Fructose is a simple sugar; the others are di- or polysaccharides.

questions.q: In which type of bond are electrons SHARED?
questions.e: Covalent bonds: nonmetals share electrons.

questions.q: In which type of bond does one atom take ('steal') electrons from another?
questions.e: Ionic: electrons are given by one atom and received by another.

questions.q: In water, oxygen and hydrogen share electrons UNEQUALLY. This is a:
questions.e: Polar covalent = unequal sharing (e.g., water).

questions.q: Sharing electrons equally between atoms of about the same size is a:
questions.e: Nonpolar covalent = equal sharing (e.g., CO₂).

questions.q: Covalent bonds form between:
w: A metal and a nonmetal transferring electrons
questions.e: Covalent = two or more nonmetals sharing.

questions.q: Polar covalent bonds share electrons unequally because:
questions.a: The atoms are very different in size
w: The atoms are the same size
questions.e: Large difference in atom size → unequal sharing.

questions.q: When Na gives its electron to Cl to form NaCl, the bond formed is:
questions.e: Electron transferred (not shared), so it's ionic.

questions.q: A chemical bond is an attraction between atoms created by:
questions.e: Bonds form by sharing, losing or gaining electrons.

questions.q: AB + CD → AC + BD is an example of:
questions.e: Partners are swapped, so it's an exchange reaction.

questions.q: A + B + energy ⇄ AB is an example of a:
questions.e: The double arrow means either direction.

questions.q: A + B → AB is an example of:
questions.e: Putting pieces together = synthesis.

questions.q: A + BC → AC + B is an example of:
questions.e: One element replaces another in a compound.

questions.q: AB → A + B + energy is an example of:
questions.e: Breaking down, releasing energy = decomposition (catabolic).

questions.q: A double displacement reaction is actually a combination of which two reactions?
questions.e: AB + CD breaks apart (catabolic) and then recombines (anabolic).

questions.q: Metal on a car slowly rusting is the lecture's example of a:
questions.e: Most reactions in nature are reversible, even if it takes years.

questions.q: Which statement about reversible reactions is TRUE?
questions.a: Most reactions in nature are reversible
questions.e: Most natural reactions are reversible.

questions.q: Which substance is known as the 'universal solvent'?
questions.e: Water is the universal solvent.

questions.q: Water makes up about how much of your body weight?
questions.e: ~2/3 of body weight.

questions.q: A solvent is a substance that:
questions.e: Solvent: dissolves things.

questions.q: Water is held together by which type of bond?
questions.e: Water is an inorganic compound with polar covalent bonds.

questions.q: Water is classified as a(n):
questions.e: Water contains no carbon, so it is inorganic.

questions.q: Which is NOT a function of water in the body?
questions.e: Water: solvent, lubrication/cushioning, temperature regulation, transport. DNA stores genetic info.

questions.q: Water helps regulate body temperature through:
questions.a: Sweat and its high heat capacity
questions.e: Temperature regulator: sweat and high heat capacity.

questions.q: Why is water called the 'universal solvent'?
questions.a: It dissolves more substances than any other liquid
w: It is found everywhere in the universe
questions.e: Water's polarity lets it dissolve a huge range of substances.

questions.q: Which term does NOT refer to the head?
questions.e: Caudal = toward the tail.

questions.q: Which term means 'toward the tail'?
questions.e: Caudad/caudal/inferior = tail.

questions.q: 'Cephalic' refers to the:
questions.e: Cephalon = head.

questions.q: Which term does NOT refer to the tail/feet?
questions.e: Cranial = toward the head.

questions.q: Which group contains ONLY 'head' words?
questions.e: Head: superior, cranial, cephalic.

questions.q: Which group contains ONLY 'tail' words?
questions.e: Tail: inferior, caudal, caudad.

questions.q: 'Cephalon' is the Latin/Greek word for:
questions.e: Cephalon (head) → 'cephalic'. Cranium = skull.

questions.q: The feet are ______ to the head.
questions.e: Toward the tail/feet = inferior/caudal.

questions.q: The pH scale ranges from:
questions.e: pH range is 0–14.

questions.q: The normal pH of human blood is:
questions.e: Blood pH = 7.35–7.45 (slightly basic).

questions.q: As H⁺ concentration INCREASES, a solution becomes more:
questions.e: More H⁺ = more acidic = lower pH.

questions.q: As OH⁻ concentration INCREASES, a solution becomes more:
questions.e: More OH⁻ = more basic = higher pH.

questions.q: Human blood (pH 7.35–7.45) is:
questions.e: Just above 7 = slightly basic.

questions.q: Osmosis is the movement of:
w: Gases from high to low concentration
Particles through holes driven by blood pressure
questions.e: Osmosis = 'the diffusion of water'.

questions.q: Simple diffusion is the movement of molecules:
questions.a: From high to low concentration without energy
w: From low to high concentration using ATP
questions.e: Diffusion: high → low, down a concentration gradient, no energy.

questions.q: What is the key difference between diffusion and osmosis?
questions.a: Osmosis moves only water; diffusion moves other molecules
w: Diffusion requires ATP; osmosis does not
Diffusion moves low to high; osmosis high to low
Osmosis is active; diffusion is passive
questions.e: Both are passive and high → low; osmosis is water only.

questions.q: Diffusion and osmosis are both examples of:
questions.e: Both are passive.

questions.q: A cell placed in a HYPOTONIC solution will:
questions.e: Water rushes in, so the cell swells.

questions.q: A cell placed in a HYPERTONIC solution will:
questions.e: Water moves out, so the cell shrinks.

questions.q: In an ISOTONIC solution, a cell will:
questions.e: Same concentration inside and out, so water moves evenly.

questions.q: Simple diffusion is driven by:
questions.e: Diffusion is driven by a concentration gradient.

questions.q: The sagittal plane divides the body into:
questions.e: Sagittal = left/right.

questions.q: The frontal plane is another name for the:
questions.e: Coronal a.k.a. frontal.

questions.q: Which plane is also called the angular plane?
questions.e: Oblique = angular.

questions.q: A cut that separates the face from the back of the head is along the:
questions.e: Front vs. back = coronal (frontal).

questions.q: A cut that separates the right eye from the left eye is along a:
questions.e: Left vs. right = sagittal.

questions.q: A cut at the waist separating the upper body from the lower body is along the:
questions.e: Top vs. bottom = transverse (horizontal).

questions.q: The median plane is another name for the:
questions.e: Midsagittal (median).

questions.q: Which pairing is correct?
questions.e: Coronal splits front/back; sagittal splits left/right.

questions.q: 'Medial' means:
w: Close to the point of attachment
questions.e: Medial = toward the midline.

questions.q: The wrist is ______ to the elbow.
questions.e: Distal = farther from the point of attachment.

questions.q: The ears are ______ to the nose.
questions.e: Lateral = away from the midline.

questions.q: The elbow is ______ to the wrist.
questions.e: Proximal = closer to the point of attachment.

questions.q: 'Superficial' means:
questions.e: Superficial (external) = toward the surface.

questions.q: The skin is ______ to the muscles.
questions.e: The skin is closer to the surface.

questions.q: 'Anterior' is also called:
questions.e: Anterior (ventral) = toward the front.

questions.q: 'Posterior' is also called:
questions.e: Posterior (dorsal) = toward the back.

questions.q: The nose is ______ to the eyes.
questions.e: The nose is closer to the midline.

questions.q: The term for 'between superficial and deep' is:
questions.e: Intermediate = between superficial and deep.

questions.q: Which statement about synthesis reactions is TRUE?
questions.a: They build larger molecules and require energy
questions.e: Synthesis (anabolic) = construction; requires energy.

questions.q: Dehydration synthesis creates a bond by:
questions.e: Dehydration = removal of water.

questions.q: Synthesis reactions are also called:
questions.e: Synthesis = anabolic; decomposition = catabolic.

questions.q: Which equation represents a synthesis reaction?
questions.e: Synthesis puts A and B together into AB.

questions.q: The lecture describes synthesis as:
questions.e: Synthesis = construction; decomposition = demolition.

questions.q: Energy for a synthesis reaction usually comes in the form of:
questions.e: Requires energy input, usually heat.

questions.q: Forming functional proteins from amino acids is an example of:
questions.e: Building proteins = synthesis.

questions.q: The OPPOSITE of dehydration synthesis is:
questions.a: Hydrolysis (breaking a bond by adding water)
questions.e: Hydrolysis = break by adding water.
